# Exploratory Data Analysis {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## What is EDA?

-   First step in any data analysis
-   Understand structure and patterns in your data
-   Identify outliers, missing values, errors
-   Generate hypotheses for formal testing

::: callout-tip
## Always visualize your data before running statistical tests!
:::

## Key dplyr Verbs

-   `dpylr` is a package in the `tidyverse` that gives you functions (aka verbs) to wrangle data.

| Verb          | Purpose                | Example                         |
|:--------------|:-----------------------|:--------------------------------|
| `filter()`    | Subset rows by values  | `filter(df, x > 5)`             |
| `select()`    | Subset columns by name | `select(df, col1, col2)`        |
| `arrange()`   | Reorder rows           | `arrange(df, x)`                |
| `mutate()`    | Create new columns     | `mutate(df, z = x + y)`         |
| `summarise()` | Collapse to summary    | `summarise(df, mean = mean(x))` |

## Filter, Arrange, and Select

```{r}
#| label: week2-filter-arrange-select
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Filter rows
filter(flights, month == 11 | month == 12)

# Arrange rows
arrange(flights, year, month, day)

# Select columns
select(flights, year, month, day)
```

![](images/week_02_S14_boolean_set_operations_venn.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

## Conditional Operators

| Operator  | Meaning                 |
|:----------|:------------------------|
| `==`      | Equals exactly          |
| `<`, `<=` | Less than (or equal)    |
| `>`, `>=` | Greater than (or equal) |
| `!=`      | Not equal to            |
| `!`       | NOT operator            |
| `&`       | AND operator            |
| `|`       | OR operator             |
| `%in%`    | Belongs to set          |

## Mutate and Transmute

```{r}
#| label: week2-mutate-example
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Add new columns based on existing ones
mutate(flights,
  gain = arr_delay - dep_delay,
  hours = air_time / 60,
  gain_per_hour = gain / hours
)

# Using pipes
flights |>
  mutate(
    gain = arr_delay - dep_delay,
    speed = distance / air_time * 60
  )
```

## Group By and Summarise

```{r}
#| label: week2-groupby-summarise
#| eval: false
#| echo: true

# Group by categorical variable
by_day <- group_by(flights, year, month, day)

# Summarise within groups
summarise(by_day, delay = mean(dep_delay, na.rm = TRUE))
```

::: callout-warning
Aggregation functions return NA if any input value is NA. Use `na.rm = TRUE` to remove missing values.
:::

## Other Useful dplyr Functions

| Function     | Purpose                  |
|:-------------|:-------------------------|
| `slice()`    | Subset rows by position  |
| `pull()`     | Extract column as vector |
| `count()`    | Count observations       |
| `distinct()` | Unique observations      |

## Boxplots

![](images/week_02_S25_boxplot.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## DRAFT: Boxplot Anatomy with Normal Distribution

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

library(ggplot2)

# Generate normal data
set.seed(42)
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x)

# Key quantiles
q1 <- qnorm(0.25)
q3 <- qnorm(0.75)
iqr <- q3 - q1
lower_whisker <- q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_whisker <- q3 + 1.5 * iqr

par(mar = c(4, 1, 1, 1))
layout(matrix(c(1, 2), nrow = 2), heights = c(1, 2))

# Top panel: boxplot
par(mar = c(0, 4, 2, 4))
boxplot(rnorm(10000), horizontal = TRUE, ylim = c(-4, 4),
        col = "white", border = "darkred", lwd = 2, axes = FALSE,
        outline = FALSE, boxwex = 0.6)
text(0, 1.35, "Median", cex = 1.1, col = "darkred")
text(q1, 1.35, "Q1", cex = 1.1, col = "darkred")
text(q3, 1.35, "Q3", cex = 1.1, col = "darkred")
text((q1 + q3) / 2, 0.55, "IQR", cex = 1.1, col = "darkred")
text(lower_whisker, 1.35, "Q1 − 1.5×IQR", cex = 0.9, col = "darkred")
text(upper_whisker, 1.35, "Q3 + 1.5×IQR", cex = 0.9, col = "darkred")

# Bottom panel: normal curve with shading
par(mar = c(4, 4, 0, 4))
plot(x, y, type = "n", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
     xlim = c(-4, 4), ylim = c(0, max(y) * 1.15))

# Shade the IQR (50%)
x_iqr <- x[x >= q1 & x <= q3]
polygon(c(q1, x_iqr, q3), c(0, dnorm(x_iqr), 0),
        col = rgb(0.4, 0.5, 0.8, 0.5), border = NA)
# Shade Q1-1σ to Q1 and Q3 to Q3+1σ
x_left <- x[x >= q1 - 1.5 * iqr & x < q1]
polygon(c(min(x_left), x_left, q1), c(0, dnorm(x_left), 0),
        col = rgb(0.6, 0.7, 0.9, 0.4), border = NA)
x_right <- x[x > q3 & x <= q3 + 1.5 * iqr]
polygon(c(q3, x_right, max(x_right)), c(0, dnorm(x_right), 0),
        col = rgb(0.6, 0.7, 0.9, 0.4), border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 3, col = "darkred")

# Sigma labels on x-axis
axis(1, at = -4:4, labels = paste0(c("-4σ","-3σ","-2σ","-1σ","0σ",
                                      "1σ","2σ","3σ","4σ")), cex.axis = 1.1)

# Percentage labels
text(0, 0.15, "50%", cex = 1.3, col = "darkred", font = 2)
text(-1.35, 0.06, "24.65%", cex = 1.1, col = "darkred")
text(1.35, 0.06, "24.65%", cex = 1.1, col = "darkred")

# Sigma boundary labels
abline(v = c(q1, q3, lower_whisker, upper_whisker),
       lty = 3, col = "gray50")
text(q1, max(y) * 1.1, expression(-0.6745*sigma), cex = 0.9)
text(q3, max(y) * 1.1, expression(0.6745*sigma), cex = 0.9)
text(lower_whisker, max(y) * 1.1, expression(-2.698*sigma), cex = 0.9)
text(upper_whisker, max(y) * 1.1, expression(2.698*sigma), cex = 0.9)
```

> "Graphical excellence is that which gives to the viewer the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time with the least ink in the smallest space"
>

-   Show the data
-   Encourage the eye to compare differences
-   Represent magnitudes honestly and accurately
-   Draw graphical elements clearly, minimizing clutter
-   Make displays easy to interpret

# Parameters and Statistics {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Population vs. Sample

| Concept    | Population           | Sample               |
|:-----------|:---------------------|:---------------------|
| Definition | All individuals      | Subset of population |
| Parameters | μ (mean), σ (SD)     | x̄ (mean), s (SD)     |
| Goal       | What we want to know | What we can measure  |

::: callout-important
We use sample statistics to **estimate** population parameters
:::

## Accuracy vs. Precision

![](images/week_02_S51_precision_vs_accuracy_target.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="50%"}

-   **Accuracy**: closeness to true value
-   **Precision**: closeness of repeated estimates to each other
-   **Replication** quantifies variation
-   **Randomization** avoids bias

## Stochastic Processes in Statistics

-   We often want to know truths about the world, but can only estimate them
-   Uncertainty in those estimates is a given
-   Statistics is largely about quantifying and managing uncertainty
-   Random variables are products of stochastic processes
-   Expectations are based on theoretical probability distributions

## Two Interpretations of Probability

**Frequency interpretation:**

"Probabilities are mathematically convenient approximations to long run relative frequencies."

**Subjective (Bayesian) interpretation:**

"A probability statement expresses the opinion of some individual regarding how certain an event is to occur."

## Random Variables and Probability

-   **Probability** is the expression of belief in some future outcome
-   A **random variable** can take on different values with different probabilities
-   The **sample space** is the universe of all possible values
-   Sample space represented by:
    -   **Probability mass distribution** (discrete)
    -   **Probability density function** (continuous)

::: callout-important
Probabilities of a sample space **always sum to 1.0**
:::

## Probability Rules

**'And' rule (multiplication):**

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$Pr(X \text{ and } Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)$$

### LaTeX

``` text
Pr(X \text{ and } Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)
```
:::

**'Or' rule (addition):**

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$Pr(X \text{ or } Y) = Pr(X) + Pr(Y)$$

### LaTeX

``` text
Pr(X \text{ or } Y) = Pr(X) + Pr(Y)
```
:::

::: callout-note
The 'and' rule assumes independent events. For non-independent events, we need conditional probabilities.
:::

## Joint and Conditional Probability

**Joint probability (independent events):**

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$Pr(X,Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)$$

### LaTeX

``` text
Pr(X,Y) = Pr(X) \times Pr(Y)
```
:::

**Conditional probability (independent):**

$$Pr(Y|X) = Pr(Y) \text{ and } Pr(X|Y) = Pr(X)$$

**Conditional probability (non-independent):**

$$Pr(Y|X) \neq Pr(Y) \text{ and } Pr(X|Y) \neq Pr(X)$$

## Likelihood vs. Probability

-   **Probability**: proportion of times an event would occur over many trials
-   **Likelihood**: conditional probability of a parameter value given data

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$L[\text{parameter}|\text{data}] = Pr[\text{data}|\text{parameter}]$$

### LaTeX

``` text
L[\text{parameter}|\text{data}] = Pr[\text{data}|\text{parameter}]
```
:::

-   **Maximum likelihood**: highest value of the likelihood function
-   **Bayesian estimate**: uses prior distribution to update posterior distribution

## Moments of Distributions

**1st moment (mean/expectation):**

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$E[X] = \sum_{\text{all x}}xP(X=x) = \mu$$

### LaTeX

``` text
E[X] = \sum_{\text{all x}}xP(X=x) = \mu
```
:::

**2nd moment (variance):**

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$Var(X) = E[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2$$

### LaTeX

``` text
Var(X) = E[(X-\mu)^2] = \sigma^2
```
:::

**Standard deviation:** $$SD = \sqrt{\sigma^2} = \sigma$$

Higher moments include skewness (3rd) and kurtosis (4th).

# Discrete Probability Distributions {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## PMF, PDF, and CDF in R

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmf-pdf-cdf-output
#| fig-cap: "Comparing discrete (Poisson) and continuous (Normal) distributions (probability mass function, probability density function, and cumulative density function)"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# Discrete (Poisson) PMF
x_disc <- 0:15
plot(x_disc, dpois(x_disc, lambda = 5), type = "h", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue",
     main = "PMF: Poisson(λ=5)", xlab = "x", ylab = "P(X = x)")
points(x_disc, dpois(x_disc, lambda = 5), pch = 19, col = "steelblue")

# Continuous (Normal) PDF
x_cont <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 200)
plot(x_cont, dnorm(x_cont), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "coral",
     main = "PDF: Normal(0, 1)", xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)")

# Poisson CDF
plot(x_disc, ppois(x_disc, lambda = 5), type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     main = "CDF: Poisson(λ=5)", xlab = "x", ylab = "F(x)")

# Normal CDF
plot(x_cont, pnorm(x_cont), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "forestgreen",
     main = "CDF: Normal(0, 1)", xlab = "x", ylab = "F(x) = P(X ≤ x)")
abline(h = c(0.025, 0.975), lty = 2, col = "gray")
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: fig-pmf-pdf-cdf-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

# Discrete (Poisson) PMF
x_disc <- 0:15
plot(x_disc, dpois(x_disc, lambda = 5), type = "h", lwd = 3, col = "steelblue",
     main = "PMF: Poisson(λ=5)", xlab = "x", ylab = "P(X = x)")
points(x_disc, dpois(x_disc, lambda = 5), pch = 19, col = "steelblue")

# Continuous (Normal) PDF
x_cont <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 200)
plot(x_cont, dnorm(x_cont), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "coral",
     main = "PDF: Normal(0, 1)", xlab = "x", ylab = "f(x)")

# Poisson CDF
plot(x_disc, ppois(x_disc, lambda = 5), type = "s", lwd = 2, col = "steelblue",
     main = "CDF: Poisson(λ=5)", xlab = "x", ylab = "F(x)")

# Normal CDF
plot(x_cont, pnorm(x_cont), type = "l", lwd = 2, col = "forestgreen",
     main = "CDF: Normal(0, 1)", xlab = "x", ylab = "F(x) = P(X ≤ x)")
abline(h = c(0.025, 0.975), lty = 2, col = "gray")
```
:::

## DRAFT: Common moments of distributions

**Table 2.1** Common population parameters and sample statistics

| Parameter | Statistic | Formula |
|:----------|:----------|:--------|
| Mean ($\mu$) | $\bar{y}$ | $\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} y_i}{n}$ |
| Median | Sample median | $y_{(n+1)/2}$ if $n$ odd; $(y_{n/2} + y_{(n/2)+1})/2$ if $n$ even |
| Variance ($\sigma^2$) | $s^2$ | $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(y_i - \bar{y})^2}{n-1}$ |
| Standard deviation ($\sigma$) | $s$ | $\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{(y_i - \bar{y})^2}{n-1}}$ |
| Median absolute deviation (MAD) | Sample MAD | $\text{median}[\lvert y_i - \text{median} \rvert]$ |
| Coefficient of variation (CV) | Sample CV | $\frac{s}{\bar{y}} \times 100$ |
| Standard error of $\bar{y}$ ($\sigma_{\bar{y}}$) | $s_{\bar{y}}$ | $\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ |
| 95% confidence interval for $\mu$ | | $\bar{y} - t_{0.05(n-1)}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} \leq \mu \leq \bar{y} + t_{0.05(n-1)}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$ |

## Bernoulli Distribution

Describes the expected outcome of a single event with probability $p$.

**Example: Flipping a fair coin once**

$$Pr(X=\text{Head}) = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 = p$$

$$Pr(X=\text{Tails}) = \frac{1}{2} = 0.5 = 1 - p = q$$

Probabilities always sum to 1: $p + q = 1$

## In-Class Demo: Law of Large Numbers with Coin Flips

Watch how the proportion of heads converges to 0.5 as we flip more coins:

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: lln-coins-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

set.seed(344)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

# Different sample sizes
for(n in c(1, 8, 16, 32, 400, 1000)) {
  flips <- rbinom(n = n, size = 1, prob = 0.5)  # 0 = heads, 1 = tails
  prop_heads <- sum(flips == 0) / length(flips)
  prop_tails <- 1 - prop_heads

  barplot(height = c(prop_heads, prop_tails),
          names.arg = c("heads", "tails"),
          col = c("steelblue", "coral"),
          ylim = c(0, 1),
          main = paste("n =", n, "flips"),
          ylab = "Proportion")
  abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray")
}
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: lln-coins-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# Different sample sizes

  prop_heads <- sum(flips == 0) / length(flips)
  prop_tails <- 1 - prop_heads

  barplot(height = c(prop_heads, prop_tails),
          names.arg = c("heads", "tails"),
          col = c("steelblue", "coral"),
          ylim = c(0, 1),
          main = paste("n =", n, "flips"),
          ylab = "Proportion")
  abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray")
}
```

::: callout-tip
As sample size increases, observed proportions converge to true probability (0.5).

## Binomial Distribution

Results from combining several independent Bernoulli events.

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\large f(k) = {n \choose k} p^{k} (1-p)^{n-k}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\large f(k) = {n \choose k} p^{k} (1-p)^{n-k}
```
:::

Where:

-   $n$ = total number of trials
-   $k$ = number of successes
-   $p$ = probability of success

## Poisson Distribution

For discrete counts (e.g., snails per plot, neuron firings per second).

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$Pr(Y=r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
Pr(Y=r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^r}{r!}
```
:::

::: callout-note
The Poisson is a single-parameter distribution: $\mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda$

Variables with variance \> mean are called "overdispersed" (common in RNA-seq data).
:::

## Geometric Distribution

Probability of observing $k$ trials before the first success:

$$P(X=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$$

-   Mean = $\frac{1}{p}$
-   Variance = $\frac{(1-p)}{p^2}$

**Example:** If extinction probability is 0.1 per year, expected time to extinction?

## Negative Binomial Distribution

Probability of the $r^{th}$ success on the $k^{th}$ trial:

$$P(X=k)=\binom{k-1}{r-1}p^{r}(1-p)^{k-r}$$

-   Mean = $\frac{r}{p}$
-   Variance = $\frac{r(1-p)}{p^2}$

# Continuous Probability Distributions {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Continuous Probability Distributions

$$P(a\leq X \leq b) = \int_{a}^{b} f(x) dx$$

The indefinite integral sums to one:

$$\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x) dx = 1$$

**Expectation:** $$E[X] = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} xf(x) dx$$

## Uniform Distribution

All outcomes equally probable.

$$E[X] = \frac{(a+b)}{2}$$

## Exponential Distribution

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}
```
:::

-   $E[X] = \frac{1}{\lambda}$
-   $Var(X) = \frac{1}{\lambda^2}$

**Example:** If λ equals the instantaneous death rate, the lifespan follows an exponential distribution.

## Gamma Distribution

Waiting time until the $r^{th}$ event at rate $\lambda$:

$$f(x) = \frac{\lambda^r x^{r-1} e^{-\lambda x}}{(r-1)!}$$

-   Mean = $\frac{r}{\lambda}$
-   Variance = $\frac{r}{\lambda^2}$

**Example:** Time until 1000 DNA strands synthesized at rate 1/ms.

# The Normal or Gaussian Distribution

## Normal (Gaussian) Distribution

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
f(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}} \, \mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}}
```
:::

Notation: $v \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$

## Normal Distribution

## DRAFT: Normal Distribution - 68-95-99.7 Rule

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 1000)
y <- dnorm(x)

plot(x, y, type = "l", lwd = 3, axes = FALSE,
     xlab = "", ylab = "", ylim = c(-0.02, max(y) * 1.35))

# Shade regions
# 99.7% region
x_99 <- x[x >= -3 & x <= 3]
polygon(c(-3, x_99, 3), c(0, dnorm(x_99), 0),
        col = rgb(0.85, 0.85, 0.95, 0.5), border = NA)
# 95% region
x_95 <- x[x >= -2 & x <= 2]
polygon(c(-2, x_95, 2), c(0, dnorm(x_95), 0),
        col = rgb(0.7, 0.7, 0.9, 0.5), border = NA)
# 68% region
x_68 <- x[x >= -1 & x <= 1]
polygon(c(-1, x_68, 1), c(0, dnorm(x_68), 0),
        col = rgb(0.5, 0.5, 0.85, 0.6), border = NA)

lines(x, y, lwd = 3)

# Axis
axis(1, at = -3:3, labels = FALSE)
text(0, -0.02, "MEAN", cex = 1.2, font = 2)

# Bracket labels
arrows(-1, 0.32, 1, 0.32, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2)
text(0, 0.34, "68%", cex = 1.5, font = 2)
text(-0.5, 0.28, "One Standard\nDeviation", cex = 0.9)
text(0.5, 0.28, "One Standard\nDeviation", cex = 0.9)

arrows(-2, 0.40, 2, 0.40, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2)
text(0, 0.42, "95%", cex = 1.5, font = 2)

arrows(-3, 0.48, 3, 0.48, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2)
text(0, 0.50, "99.7%", cex = 1.5, font = 2)
```

## Why Normal is Special in Biology

![](images/week_02_S93_galton_regression_to_mean.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

## DRAFT: Galton's Regression to the Mean

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 6

# Recreate Galton's parent-offspring height data (approximate)
set.seed(1885)
n <- 200
parent_height <- rnorm(n, mean = 68, sd = 2)
offspring_height <- 29.4 + 0.57 * parent_height + rnorm(n, 0, 1.5)

# Create bubble-like effect by rounding
parent_r <- round(parent_height)
offspring_r <- round(offspring_height)

# Count duplicates for point sizing
df <- data.frame(parent = parent_r, offspring = offspring_r)
df_counts <- as.data.frame(table(df$parent, df$offspring))
names(df_counts) <- c("parent", "offspring", "count")
df_counts$parent <- as.numeric(as.character(df_counts$parent))
df_counts$offspring <- as.numeric(as.character(df_counts$offspring))
df_counts <- df_counts[df_counts$count > 0, ]

plot(df_counts$parent, df_counts$offspring,
     cex = sqrt(df_counts$count) * 1.2,
     pch = 16, col = rgb(0.3, 0.3, 0.3, 0.7),
     xlab = "AVERAGE HEIGHT OF PARENTS (IN)",
     ylab = "HEIGHT OF OFFSPRING (IN)",
     xlim = c(63, 73), ylim = c(62, 73),
     las = 1)

# Regression line
abline(a = 29.4, b = 0.57, lwd = 2)
# 1:1 line (dashed)
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lwd = 2, lty = 2)

text(64, 72, "y = 29.4 + 0.57x", cex = 1.1)
```

## Z-Scores of Normal distributions

Standardize variables to mean = 0, SD = 1:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\huge z_i = \frac{(x_i - \bar{x})}{s}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\huge z_i = \frac{(x_i - \bar{x})}{s}
```
:::

This is the **standard normal distribution**.

# Sampling from distributions in R

## Distribution Functions in R

| Prefix | Function                 | Example              |
|:-------|:-------------------------|:---------------------|
| `d`    | Probability density/mass | `dnorm(0, 0, 1)`     |
| `p`    | Cumulative distribution  | `pnorm(1.96, 0, 1)`  |
| `q`    | Quantile function        | `qnorm(0.975, 0, 1)` |
| `r`    | Random number generator  | `rnorm(100, 0, 1)`   |

Works for: `binom`, `pois`, `exp`, `norm`, `geom`, `nbinom`, `unif`, `gamma`

# Estimates and Confidence Intervals {background-color="#2c3e50"}

## Parameter Estimation

-   Estimation infers population parameters from sample data
-   Sample estimates rarely equal population parameters exactly
-   **Sampling distribution**: all values we might obtain from samples
-   **Standard error**: standard deviation of sampling distribution

::: callout-important
NO ESTIMATE IS USEFUL WITHOUT A STANDARD ERROR!
:::

## Estimation Approaches

| Approach | Description |
|:---|:---|
| **Parametric** | Assumes specific distributions |
| **Resampling** | Bootstrap/randomization for empirical distributions |
| **OLS** | Ordinary Least Squares optimization |
| **Maximum Likelihood** | Model-based estimates with confidence |
| **Bayesian** | Incorporates prior information |

## The Central Limit Theorem

For most data, we can't determine sampling distributions empirically.

The CLT tells us that the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as sample size increases, regardless of the underlying distribution.

## Visualizing the Central Limit Theorem

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: fig-clt-figure
#| fig-cap: "CLT: Sample means become normal even from non-normal populations"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

par(mfrow = c(2, 4))

# Exponential distribution (skewed)
set.seed(42)
exp_pop <- rexp(10000, rate = 1)
hist(exp_pop, main = "Population\n(Exponential)", col = "lightgray",
     border = "white", xlab = "Value", breaks = 30)

# Sample means for different n
for(n in c(5, 30, 100)) {
  means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(exp_pop, n, replace = TRUE)))
  hist(means, main = paste("Sample Means\n(n =", n, ")"),
       col = "steelblue", border = "white", xlab = "Mean", breaks = 25)
}

# Uniform distribution
unif_pop <- runif(10000, 0, 1)
hist(unif_pop, main = "Population\n(Uniform)", col = "lightgray",
     border = "white", xlab = "Value", breaks = 30)

for(n in c(5, 30, 100)) {
  means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(unif_pop, n, replace = TRUE)))
  hist(means, main = paste("Sample Means\n(n =", n, ")"),
       col = "coral", border = "white", xlab = "Mean", breaks = 25)
}
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: fig-clt-code
#| fig-cap: "CLT: Sample means become normal even from non-normal populations"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

par(mfrow = c(2, 4))

# Exponential distribution (skewed)
set.seed(42)
exp_pop <- rexp(10000, rate = 1)
hist(exp_pop, main = "Population\n(Exponential)", col = "lightgray",
     border = "white", xlab = "Value", breaks = 30)

# Sample means for different n
for(n in c(5, 30, 100)) {
  means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(exp_pop, n, replace = TRUE)))
  hist(means, main = paste("Sample Means\n(n =", n, ")"),
       col = "steelblue", border = "white", xlab = "Mean", breaks = 25)
}

# Uniform distribution
unif_pop <- runif(10000, 0, 1)
hist(unif_pop, main = "Population\n(Uniform)", col = "lightgray",
     border = "white", xlab = "Value", breaks = 30)

for(n in c(5, 30, 100)) {
  means <- replicate(1000, mean(sample(unif_pop, n, replace = TRUE)))
  hist(means, main = paste("Sample Means\n(n =", n, ")"),
       col = "coral", border = "white", xlab = "Mean", breaks = 25)
}
```
:::

## CLT in Quantitative Genetics

**Why are complex traits normally distributed?**

Simulate a trait controlled by 5 genes, each with additive effects:

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: clt-genetics-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

set.seed(245)
n_individuals <- 100

# Each locus contributes -1, 0, or +1 to phenotype (diploid genotypes)
contributions <- matrix(0, nrow = n_individuals, ncol = 5)
for(locus in 1:5) {
  genotype <- rbinom(n_individuals, size = 2, prob = 0.5)  # 0, 1, or 2 copies
  contributions[, locus] <- ifelse(genotype == 2, 1,
                                    ifelse(genotype == 1, 0, -1))
}

# Sum across loci to get phenotype
phenotype <- rowSums(contributions)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(phenotype, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "5-Locus Trait Distribution",
     xlab = "Phenotype Value", breaks = seq(-6, 6, 1))

# Add environmental noise to make continuous
phenotype_continuous <- phenotype + rnorm(n_individuals, 0, 0.5)
hist(phenotype_continuous, col = "coral", border = "white",
     main = "With Environmental Variation",
     xlab = "Phenotype Value", breaks = 20)
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: clt-genetics-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

set.seed(245)
n_individuals <- 100

# Each locus contributes -1, 0, or +1 to phenotype (diploid genotypes)
contributions <- matrix(0, nrow = n_individuals, ncol = 5)
for(locus in 1:5) {
  genotype <- rbinom(n_individuals, size = 2, prob = 0.5)  # 0, 1, or 2 copies
  contributions[, locus] <- ifelse(genotype == 2, 1,
                                    ifelse(genotype == 1, 0, -1))
}

# Sum across loci to get phenotype
phenotype <- rowSums(contributions)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
hist(phenotype, col = "steelblue", border = "white",
     main = "5-Locus Trait Distribution",
     xlab = "Phenotype Value", breaks = seq(-6, 6, 1))

# Add environmental noise to make continuous
phenotype_continuous <- phenotype + rnorm(n_individuals, 0, 0.5)
hist(phenotype_continuous, col = "coral", border = "white",
     main = "With Environmental Variation",
     xlab = "Phenotype Value", breaks = 20)
```
:::

::: callout-note
This is why quantitative traits (height, weight, blood pressure) are approximately normal!
:::

# Sampling variation of a parameter estimate

## Sampling Variation of a Parameter

![](images/week_02_S106_population_vs_sampling_distribution.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## DRAFT: Population vs Sampling Distribution

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Simulate gene length data (right-skewed gamma)
set.seed(42)
pop_data <- rgamma(100000, shape = 2.5, rate = 0.001)
pop_data <- pop_data[pop_data <= 15000]
pop_mean <- mean(pop_data)

# Sampling distribution: means of samples of n=100
sample_means <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(pop_data, 100)))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))

# Left: Population distribution
hist(pop_data, breaks = seq(0, 15000, by = 500),
     col = "#CC6633", border = "#CC6633",
     main = "Population Distribution",
     xlab = "Gene length (no. nucleotides)", ylab = "Probability",
     freq = FALSE, las = 1)

# Right: Sampling distribution
hist(sample_means, breaks = 40,
     col = "#CC6633", border = "#CC6633",
     main = "Sampling Distribution",
     xlab = expression("Sample mean length " * bar(Y) * " (nucleotides)"),
     ylab = "Probability", freq = FALSE, las = 1)
```

##

![](images/week_02_S112_standard_error_confidence_interval.jpeg){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## DRAFT: Standard Error and Confidence Intervals

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| eval: true
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 8

set.seed(42)
pop_data <- rgamma(100000, shape = 2.5, rate = 0.001)
pop_data <- pop_data[pop_data <= 15000]
pop_mean <- mean(pop_data)
sample_means <- replicate(10000, mean(sample(pop_data, 100)))
se <- sd(sample_means)

par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))

# Top-left: sampling distribution + SE arrow
hist(sample_means, breaks = 40, col = "#CC6633", border = "#CC6633",
     main = "", xlim = c(1500, 4000),
     xlab = expression("Sample mean length " * bar(X) * " (nucleotides)"),
     ylab = "Probability", freq = FALSE, las = 1)
arrows(pop_mean - se, 0.012, pop_mean + se, 0.012,
       code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2)
text(pop_mean, 0.0135, expression(sigma[bar(X)]), cex = 1.3)
text(3200, 0.008, "The standard error is the\nstandard deviation of the\nsampling distribution", cex = 0.9)

# Top-right: sampling distribution + 2SE bracket
hist(sample_means, breaks = 40, col = "#CC6633", border = "#CC6633",
     main = "", xlim = c(1500, 4000),
     xlab = expression("Sample mean length " * bar(X) * " (nucleotides)"),
     ylab = "Probability", freq = FALSE, las = 1)
arrows(pop_mean - 2*se, 0.012, pop_mean + 2*se, 0.012,
       code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2)
text(pop_mean, 0.0135, expression(sigma[bar(X)]), cex = 1.3)
text(3200, 0.008, "Roughly 95% of sample\nestimates lie within\n2 standard errors of\nthe true parameter value",
     cex = 0.9)

# Bottom-left: single sample + arrow to mu
plot(1, 1, type = "n", xlim = c(1500, 4000), ylim = c(0, 50),
     xlab = expression("Sample mean length " * bar(X) * " (nucleotides)"),
     ylab = "Frequency", las = 1, main = "")
segments(2411, 0, 2411, 1, lwd = 8, col = "#CC6633")
arrows(2411, 15, pop_mean, 15, code = 3, length = 0.1, lwd = 2)
abline(v = pop_mean, lty = 2)
text(pop_mean, 18, expression(mu), cex = 1.3)
text(2411, -3, expression(bar(X)), cex = 1.3)
text(3000, 35, "It tells us how far, on\naverage, we are from the\nparameter that we are\nattempting to estimate",
     cex = 0.9)

# Bottom-right: single sample + CI brackets
plot(1, 1, type = "n", xlim = c(1500, 4000), ylim = c(0, 50),
     xlab = expression("Sample mean length " * bar(X) * " (nucleotides)"),
     ylab = "Frequency", las = 1, main = "")
segments(2411, 0, 2411, 1, lwd = 8, col = "#CC6633")
abline(v = pop_mean, lty = 2)
text(pop_mean, 18, expression(mu), cex = 1.3)
text(2411, -3, expression(bar(X)), cex = 1.3)
# CI brackets
segments(2411 - 2*se, 5, 2411 + 2*se, 5, lwd = 2)
segments(2411 - 2*se, 3, 2411 - 2*se, 7, lwd = 2)
segments(2411 + 2*se, 3, 2411 + 2*se, 7, lwd = 2)
text(3200, 35, "Therefore, lines extending\n2 standard errors outward\nfrom the sample estimate\nwill bracket the true parameter\nin roughly 95% of samples",
     cex = 0.85)
```

## Standard Error of the Mean

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$\huge \sigma_{\bar{x}} \approx s_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}$$

### LaTeX

``` text
\huge \sigma_{\bar{x}} \approx s_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
```
:::

::: callout-note
-   SEM is NOT the standard deviation of the original distribution
-   SEM decreases as sample size increases
:::

## Calculating SEM

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: sem-calc-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

set.seed(32)
true_pop <- rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 2, sd = 5)

# Small sample
samps_5 <- replicate(n = 50, sample(true_pop, size = 5))
sem_5 <- sd(apply(samps_5, 2, mean)) / sqrt(50)

# Larger sample
samps_50 <- replicate(n = 50, sample(true_pop, size = 50))
sem_50 <- sd(apply(samps_50, 2, mean)) / sqrt(50)

cat("SEM (n=5):", round(sem_5, 4), "\nSEM (n=50):", round(sem_50, 4))
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: sem-calc-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

set.seed(32)
true_pop <- rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 2, sd = 5)

# Small sample
samps_5 <- replicate(n = 50, sample(true_pop, size = 5))
sem_5 <- sd(apply(samps_5, 2, mean)) / sqrt(50)

# Larger sample
samps_50 <- replicate(n = 50, sample(true_pop, size = 50))
sem_50 <- sd(apply(samps_50, 2, mean)) / sqrt(50)

cat("SEM (n=5):", round(sem_5, 4), "\nSEM (n=50):", round(sem_50, 4))
```
:::

## Confidence Intervals

A confidence interval is a range of values about a parameter estimate such that we are X% certain the true population parameter lies within.

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: conf-int-output
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

# 95% CI using t.test
sample_data <- rnorm(30, mean = 10, sd = 2)
t.test(sample_data)$conf.int
```

### Code

```{r}
#| label: conf-int-code
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

# 95% CI using t.test
sample_data <- rnorm(30, mean = 10, sd = 2)
t.test(sample_data)$conf.int
```
:::

## Visualizing What "95% Confidence" Means

::: panel-tabset
### Output

```{r}
#| label: fig-ci-demo-code
#| fig-cap: "95% of CIs from repeated sampling contain the true mean (μ = 10)"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
#| echo: false
#| eval: true

true_mean <- 10
n_samples <- 50

# Take 50 samples and calculate CIs
results <- t(replicate(n_samples, {
  samp <- rnorm(20, mean = true_mean, sd = 2)
  ci <- t.test(samp)$conf.int
  c(mean = mean(samp), lower = ci[1], upper = ci[2])
}))

# Plot CIs - color red if they miss the true mean
contains_true <- results[, "lower"] <= true_mean & results[, "upper"] >= true_mean
colors <- ifelse(contains_true, "steelblue", "red")

plot(NULL, xlim = c(8, 12), ylim = c(0, n_samples + 1),
     xlab = "Value", ylab = "Sample Number", main = "50 Confidence Intervals")
abline(v = true_mean, col = "darkgreen", lwd = 2)
for(i in 1:n_samples) {
  segments(results[i, "lower"], i, results[i, "upper"], i, col = colors[i], lwd = 2)
  points(results[i, "mean"], i, pch = 19, cex = 0.6, col = colors[i])
}
legend("topright", c(paste(sum(contains_true), "contain μ"),
       paste(sum(!contains_true), "miss μ")), col = c("steelblue", "red"), lwd = 2)
```

### Code


## Coefficient of Variation

To compare standard deviations across populations with different means:

::: panel-tabset
### Equation

$$CV = \frac{s}{\bar{x}} \times 100\%$$

### LaTeX

``` text
CV = \frac{s}{\bar{x}} \times 100\%
```
:::
